questions.q: What four jobs does a real, production-shaped event listener service do that a bare `contract.on(...)` call alone does not?
options: Connect through a resilient provider, catch up on missed events, listen live, and confirm before treating events as final
Compile the contract, deploy it, verify it, and audit it
Mint new tokens, burn tokens, pause the contract, and transfer ownership
Encrypt the RPC endpoint, rotate API keys, log in a user, and send an email
questions.explain: A raw .on() call only covers 'listen live' — a real service also needs a resilient connection, a backfill step for downtime, and a confirmation gate before acting on anything.

questions.q: What breaks if a listener service doesn't persist its last-processed block?
options: Every restart silently starts the live listener from "now," losing any events that happened while the service was offline
The service refuses to start at all
Gas costs increase for every transaction the contract processes
The contract's ABI becomes invalid
questions.explain: Without a persisted checkpoint, there's no way to know what range of blocks to backfill on restart, so anything missed during downtime is silently lost.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, why does `handleTransfer` check the number of confirmations before logging/saving progress?
options: To avoid treating an event as final when a reorg could still remove the block it came from
Because Etherscan requires at least 5 confirmations to display any transaction
To reduce the gas cost of the Transfer event itself
Confirmations are checked only for events involving native ETH, never ERC-20 tokens
questions.explain: This is Lesson 9's confirmation gate applied in practice — skip acting on an event until enough blocks have been built on top of it.

questions.q: Why does the example use the exact same `handleTransfer` function for both backfilled (missed) events and live events?
options: Because backfilled history and live events are the same kind of data — there's no reason to process them differently
Because live events must always be processed before backfilled ones
Because ethers.js requires a separate function signature for queryFilter results
It doesn't — the lesson uses two unrelated handlers for the two cases
questions.explain: Whether an event arrives via a one-shot queryFilter backfill or a live .on() callback, it's the same kind of event and deserves the same confirmation-gated handling.

questions.q: What does this lesson explicitly say is left out of its simple version, as honest next steps toward production-readiness?
options: Reorg detection during the confirmation wait, deduplicating events across the backfill/live boundary, and using a real database instead of a flat file
Nothing — the example is already fully production-ready as written
Support for ERC-20 tokens, which the example claims is impossible
The ability to connect to more than one RPC provider
questions.explain: The guide is explicit that block-hash-based reorg detection, event deduplication, and a real database are the honest next steps this simplified version doesn't cover.
